resources.label: Learn C#
resources.note: Our C# practice site. Type each example in, run it, and change it. C# is one of the languages AQA accepts in the exam.

tips.title: A function returns, a procedure does not
tips.body: If it sends a value back with `RETURN`, it is a **function**. If it just does something, it is a **procedure**. Outputting inside a function instead of returning is the classic error.

tips.title: Local names die with the subroutine
tips.body: A variable created inside a subroutine exists only while it runs. Assigning to it does **not** change a variable of the same name outside, which is what a tracing question is usually testing.

tips.title: Every branch needs a RETURN
tips.body: If a function returns inside an `IF` but not in the `ELSE`, it sometimes returns nothing. Check every path through the code ends in a value.

tips.title: AQA says parameter for both
tips.body: Some books distinguish an argument in the call from a parameter in the header. AQA states that in examinable material it uses **parameter** for both, so do not lose time on a distinction the board does not examine.

why.matters:
A subroutine is a block of code with a **name**, and naming something is what lets you stop thinking about it. Once `is_even(n)` exists and works, the rest of the program can use it without anyone reading it again.

That is how a program gets big enough to be useful without getting too big to hold in your head. It also decides where a change goes: one definition, one place to edit, one place to test. The exam calls this **structured programming**, and the two words to keep apart are *procedure*, which does a job, and *function*, which hands a value back.

examples.title: Why the pass mark should live in one place
examples.body:
A program that checks a pass mark in 14 places has the number 50 written 14 times. The day the pass mark moves to 45, 13 of them get changed and the last one is found in November by somebody who was told they failed.

Written as a subroutine — one `has_passed(mark)` that everything calls — the change is a single line, and every part of the program that uses it is right from the moment it is saved. That is the argument worth making in an answer, and it is worth more than *it makes the code tidy*.

visual.alt: A table comparing a pass mark written out fourteen times with the same rule written once as a subroutine: fourteen places to edit and test against one, and a program that can end up with two different rules at once

examples.title: Why a function is a machine you hand a value to
examples.body:
`is_even(7)` is not a set of instructions at the point where you use it. It **is** `False`. A call becomes its returned value, which is why it can go straight into an `IF`, be stored in a variable, or be output.

The names in the header are **parameters**, and AQA calls the values handed in parameters too (some books call them **arguments**): `SUBROUTINE is_even(n)` has the parameter `n`, and `is_even(7)` passes it the value 7. Inside, `n` is 7 for that call only. The next call can pass 8 and get True, with nothing left over from this one.

visual.alt: A trace of a call to is_even with the value seven: the parameter n holds seven, seven MOD two is one so the IF is not taken, and the ELSE branch returns False

examples.title: Why two subroutines can both use i
examples.body:
A variable made inside a subroutine is **local**: it exists while that subroutine is running and is gone afterwards, and nothing outside can see it. So every subroutine can have its own `i`, its own `total`, its own `temp`, and none of them collide.

A **global** is the opposite — visible everywhere, changeable from anywhere — which sounds convenient right up to the afternoon a value is wrong and nine different parts of the program could have done it. *Where can this be changed from?* is the question that makes the difference obvious.

visual.alt: A table comparing local and global variables: a local is made inside a subroutine, lasts only while that call runs and is seen by that subroutine alone, while a global is made outside, lasts for the whole program and can be changed anywhere

steps.title: A subroutine is a named block of code
steps.body:
A **subroutine** is a block of code with a name. You write it once, then **call** it by name as many times as you like. There are two kinds:

- A **procedure** does a job, such as printing a message.
- A **function** does a job **and returns a value** to the code that called it.

AQA writes both with `SUBROUTINE ... ENDSUBROUTINE`. Here is a procedure and two calls:

```
SUBROUTINE greet(name)
   OUTPUT 'Hello ' + name
ENDSUBROUTINE

greet('Sam')
greet('Priya')
```

Output: `Hello Sam` then `Hello Priya`. The code inside runs once for each call.

steps.text: First call: name takes the value Sam, so the line outputs Hello Sam
The subroutine ends and control returns to the line after the call
Second call: name is now Priya, so the output is Hello Priya

check.prompt: How many times does the code inside `greet` run in the program above?
check.solution: Defining a subroutine runs nothing. Each call runs the body once.
options: Three times, including the definition
It never runs, because subroutines are only definitions
Twice, once for each call
Once, when the subroutine is defined

steps.title: Parameters and arguments
steps.body:
The names in the brackets of the header are **parameters**. The values you pass in when you call it are matched to them **in order**: the first value goes into the first parameter. AQA calls both of these **parameters**; some books call the values in the call **arguments**.

```
SUBROUTINE show_age(name, age)
   OUTPUT name + ' is ' + INT_TO_STRING(age)
ENDSUBROUTINE

show_age('Lee', 15)
```

Output: `Lee is 15`. Swap the two values round and the program would try to join 15 and a string in the wrong places.

visuals.alt: Trace table for the call show_age with Lee and 15: name is Lee, age is 15, output Lee is 15

visuals.problem: What happens if the call is written `show_age(15, 'Lee')`?

steps.text: The values fill the parameters left to right, so `name` takes 15 and `age` takes `'Lee'`
The body then works out `name + ' is ' + INT_TO_STRING(age)`, so it tries `INT_TO_STRING('Lee')`
steps.note: a string where an integer is expected

steps.text: `'Lee'` is not an integer, so there is nothing to convert and the program fails
steps.note: INT_TO_STRING needs an integer and 'Lee' is not one, so the program fails

steps.text: Written the right way round, `show_age('Lee', 15)` outputs `Lee is 15`
steps.note: check the call against the header every time

check.solution: Some books call the value in the call an **argument** and the name in the header a **parameter**, but AQA states that in examinable material it uses **parameter** for both. So 15 is a parameter.

markScheme.description: a parameter, the term AQA uses for both

options: A return value sent back by the subroutine
A parameter, which is what AQA calls both the value and the name
The name given in the subroutine header only
A local variable declared inside the subroutine

steps.title: Functions return a value
steps.body:
A **function** ends with `RETURN` and hands a value back. The call then **becomes** that value, so you can store it, print it, or use it in a bigger expression.

```
SUBROUTINE area(width, height)
   RETURN width * height
ENDSUBROUTINE

room ← area(4, 5)
OUTPUT room * 2
```

`area(4, 5)` returns 20, so `room` is 20 and the output is 40. Notice the function does not output anything itself. Returning is what makes it reusable: the caller decides what to do with the answer.

visuals.alt: Trace of the area program: width 4, height 5, returns 20, room is 20, output 40

check.prompt: `OUTPUT area(3, 7) + 1` is run with the same `area` function. What is output?

steps.title: Tracing a function call
steps.body:
To trace a call, write a column for every parameter and every variable inside the function, plus one for the returned value. Fill in a row each time something changes.

```
SUBROUTINE double_add(a, b)
   result ← a * 2 + b
   RETURN result
ENDSUBROUTINE

x ← double_add(3, 4)
OUTPUT x
```

`result` is a local variable, so it gets its own column too.

visuals.alt: Trace of double_add(3, 4): a 3, b 4, result 10, returns 10, x 10, output 10

steps.text: RETURN 10, so x becomes 10, and the last line outputs 10

steps.title: Local and global variables
steps.body:
A variable created **inside** a subroutine is **local**: it exists only while that subroutine runs, and nothing outside can see it. In pseudo-code and Python, a variable created in the main program is **global**; in C# and VB.NET a variable declared inside `Main` is local to `Main`, and a value shared by every method has to be a field of the class. Languages differ on what happens when a subroutine assigns to a name that **already exists outside**: in Python a new local is made unless you write `global`. In C# and VB.NET a method cannot see another method's locals at all, so the name has to be a field of the class for the outer value to change. AQA's pseudo-code does not say, so an exam question will make the rule clear, and a good answer never relies on shadowing a global. Local variables are better: two subroutines can both use a variable called `total` without clashing, and a subroutine cannot accidentally wreck a value the rest of the program depends on.

```
total ← 100

SUBROUTINE spend(amount)
   spent ← amount * 2
   OUTPUT spent
ENDSUBROUTINE

spend(5)
OUTPUT total
```

Inside `spend`, `spent` is **local**: it is created when the subroutine runs and is gone when it ends, so the main program could not output it. `total` is **global** and is never assigned to inside the subroutine, so it is still 100 at the end. The outputs are `10` then `100`.

visuals.alt: A trace of the spend program: the global total holds 100, the call spend(5) gives amount 5 and the local spent 10, which is output first, and then the unchanged global total 100 is output

check.prompt: Why are local variables preferred over global variables?
check.solution: Locals are private to their subroutine, so they cannot interfere with anything else.
options: Global variables cannot store numbers, so any calculation has to be done with local ones
A subroutine cannot accidentally change a value the rest of the program relies on, and names can be reused safely
Local variables use less memory because their names are shorter, so the program runs faster
Local variables keep their value after the subroutine ends, so nothing is lost between calls

steps.title: Your turn: write a function
steps.body:
Write a function `is_even(n)` that returns `True` if `n` is even and `False` otherwise. Plan: header with one parameter, use `MOD`, return in both cases.

Then try it for real: write `IsEven` in C# on our [Learn C#](https://red-dune-0f7372e10.7.azurestaticapps.net/) site and run it with 8 and 7.

steps.text:
```
SUBROUTINE is_even(n)
   IF n MOD 2 = 0 THEN
      RETURN True
   ELSE
      RETURN False
   ENDIF
ENDSUBROUTINE
```
A shorter version returns the comparison itself: RETURN n MOD 2 = 0
Check: is_even(8) returns True, is_even(7) returns False

check.prompt: Which line correctly uses the function to decide what to print?
check.solution: Call the function with an argument, and use the value it returns as the condition.
options: is_even(x) OUTPUT 'even'
OUTPUT is_even(x) = 'even'
IF is_even THEN OUTPUT 'even' ENDIF
IF is_even(x) THEN OUTPUT 'even' ENDIF

steps.title: Why programs are built from subroutines
steps.body:
The **structured approach** to programming means breaking a problem into parts (**decomposition**) and writing a subroutine, or module, for each, and giving each subroutine a clear, documented interface: its **parameters** say what goes in, its **return value** says what comes out, and it keeps its working in **local variables**. The benefits:

- **No repetition**: written once, called many times.
- **One change fixes every use**.
- **Easier to read**: the main program reads like a list of steps.
- **Easier to test**: each subroutine can be tested on its own.
- **Reusable**: the same subroutine can be used in another program.
- **Shared work**: different programmers can write different subroutines, because each interface says exactly what goes in and what comes back.

You already use built-in subroutines: `LEN(word)`, `RANDOM_INT(1, 6)`, `STRING_TO_INT(text)` are all functions someone else wrote.

visuals.problem: A quiz program without subroutines has the same ten lines of "ask a question, check the answer, add to score" repeated five times. Improve it.

steps.text: Write one subroutine ask(question, answer) that does those ten lines once
Call it five times with different values
If the checking needs to change, it changes in one place, and the main program is five readable lines

check.solution: LEN returns a value, so it is a function, and it is built into the language.
options: A procedure that prints the length of the name
A parameter of the main program that stores the name
A local variable that holds the length of the name
A built-in function that returns the number of characters in a string

steps.title: Going deeper: nested calls and loops inside functions
steps.body:
Exam questions stack the ideas: a function that contains a loop, or a call inside a call. Work **inside out**: evaluate the innermost call first, replace it with its value, then continue.

```
SUBROUTINE g(n)
   RETURN n + 3
ENDSUBROUTINE

SUBROUTINE f(n)
   RETURN n * n
ENDSUBROUTINE

OUTPUT f(g(2))
```

`g(2)` returns 5, so this is `f(5)`, which returns 25.

For a function with a loop, trace the loop fully inside the function before you write the returned value. Write the trace out: it shows your working, not just the answer.

```
SUBROUTINE sum_to(n)
   t ← 0
   FOR i ← 1 TO n
      t ← t + i
   ENDFOR
   RETURN t
ENDSUBROUTINE
```

visuals.alt: Trace of sum_to(4): t starts at 0, i goes 1 to 4, t becomes 1, 3, 6, 10, returns 10

check.prompt: With the functions f and g above, what is `g(f(3))`?

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A subroutine is a named block of code. A procedure does a job; a function also returns a value with RETURN.
- Parameters are the names in the header, and the values in the call are matched to them in order (AQA calls both parameters; some books call the values arguments).
- A function call becomes its returned value, so it can be stored or used in an expression.
- Variables made inside a subroutine are local. Globals belong to the main program. Prefer locals.
- The **structured approach**: one subroutine per part of the problem, each with a clear interface of parameters in, a return value out and local variables inside.
- Subroutines remove repetition, make one change fix every use, and make programs easier to read, test and reuse.
- Trace nested calls from the inside out; trace loops fully before writing the return value.

visuals.alt: A blank trace table layout: one column per variable, one for the returned value, and one for output

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a procedure and a function?
questions.solution: Both are subroutines. The one that hands a value back with RETURN is a function.
options: A function must be called from inside a loop; a procedure need not be
A procedure can have parameters; a function cannot
A function returns a value to the code that called it; a procedure does not
A procedure runs faster than a function because it is shorter

questions.prompt: Which keyword sends a value back from a function to the code that called it?
questions.solution: RETURN. In Python it is `return`; the idea is the same.
Parameters are the names in the brackets of the header. AQA also calls the values passed in the call parameters; some books call those arguments.
options: A variable declared in the main program that every subroutine can read and change
A comment written above a subroutine that explains what the subroutine does
The value a function sends back to the calling code when it reaches RETURN
A variable in a subroutine header that receives a value when the subroutine is called

questions.prompt:
What is output by the call `greet('Amy')` when `greet` is:

```
SUBROUTINE greet(name)
   OUTPUT 'Hi ' + name + '!'
ENDSUBROUTINE
```
questions.solution: The parameter `name` takes the value Amy, so the output is Hi Amy! with the exclamation mark.

questions.prompt:
What value is stored in `room` after this code runs?

```
SUBROUTINE area(width, height)
   RETURN width * height
ENDSUBROUTINE

room ← area(4, 5)
OUTPUT room * 2
```
questions.solution: `area(4, 5)` returns 4 × 5 = 20, which is assigned to `room`. The line after that outputs 40, but the question asks for `room`.

questions.prompt:
What is output by the last line of this program?

```
SUBROUTINE twice(word)
   RETURN word + word
ENDSUBROUTINE

OUTPUT twice('go') + twice('!')
```
questions.solution: `twice('go')` gives gogo and `twice('!')` gives !!. Joined together: gogo!!

questions.prompt: Explain three advantages of using subroutines in a program.
questions.solution: Any three of: no repetition, one change fixes every use, easier to read, easier to test, easier to debug, reusable in other programs, split between different programmers.

markScheme.description: Easier to read, or to test and fix one part at a time
Reusable in other programs, or can be written by different programmers

criteria.text: Code that is needed in several places is written once and called many times, so there is less repetition
A second, different advantage: each subroutine does one job, so the program is easier to read, or to test and fix one part at a time
A third, different advantage: subroutines can be reused in other programs, or written by different programmers

questions.modelAnswer: A subroutine is written once and can be called from many places, so code is not repeated and a change only has to be made in one place. Breaking a program into subroutines that each do one job makes it easier to read, easier to test one part at a time, and easier to find and fix errors. Subroutines can also be reused in other programs, and different programmers can write different subroutines at the same time.

questions.prompt: A variable is declared inside a subroutine. Which statement is correct?
questions.solution: Variables created inside a subroutine are local. They are created when the subroutine starts and destroyed when it ends.
options: It keeps its value between one call of the subroutine and the next, so the next call starts where the last one finished
It is a local variable: it exists only while the subroutine runs and cannot be seen from outside it
It is a global variable: every part of the program can read and change it
It must have the same name as one of the parameters, because a subroutine can only work with the names listed in its header

What is output by this program?

```
SUBROUTINE sum_to(n)
   t ← 0

      t ← t + i
   ENDFOR
   RETURN t
ENDSUBROUTINE

OUTPUT sum_to(4)
```

questions.solution: The loop adds 1, 2, 3 and 4 to t in turn: 0 → 1 → 3 → 6 → 10. The function returns 10.

questions.prompt: Write a function called `larger` that takes two numbers as parameters and returns the larger of the two. Then write one line that calls it with 7 and 12 and outputs the result.
questions.solution: The marks are for the header, the comparison, returning in both branches, the call, and clean structure. The RETURN marks are for handing the value back; a function that only outputs it has not done that job.

markScheme.description: Returns a when a is the larger
Returns b when b is the larger (or they are equal)
Call with 7 and 12 in an OUTPUT

criteria.text: Correct header with two parameters, for example SUBROUTINE larger(a, b)
IF statement comparing the two parameters
Returns the first parameter when it is the larger, by any correct route (a RETURN in a branch, or a local variable returned at the end)
Returns the second parameter when it is the larger or the two are equal
Call with 7 and 12 inside an OUTPUT, for example OUTPUT larger(7, 12)
Correct structure: ENDIF and ENDSUBROUTINE, and the function does not itself output

questions.modelAnswer:
```
SUBROUTINE larger(a, b)
   IF a > b THEN
      RETURN a
   ELSE
      RETURN b
   ENDIF
ENDSUBROUTINE

OUTPUT larger(7, 12)
```

questions.prompt:
What is the second value output by this program?

```
total ← 100

SUBROUTINE spend(amount)
   spent ← amount * 2
   OUTPUT spent
ENDSUBROUTINE

spend(5)
OUTPUT total
```
questions.solution: `spent` is a local variable, created inside `spend` and gone when it ends; the procedure outputs $5 \times 2 = 10$. The subroutine never assigns to `total`, so the global is untouched and the second output is **100**.

markScheme.description: spent is local, so the subroutine never changes total

questions.prompt: A programmer writes a function that calculates a total and outputs it, but never returns it. Why is this poor design?
questions.solution: Returning the value lets the caller decide what to do with it: print it, store it, compare it. Outputting inside the function fixes the behaviour for every caller.
options: A function with no RETURN statement runs forever, so the program never reaches the line that would print the total
Functions are not allowed to contain OUTPUT statements, so the program will not run at all
The calling code cannot use the total in a further calculation or store it, so the function only works for one purpose
The total will be lost when the function ends because it is a global variable, not a local one

questions.prompt:
Complete a trace table for this program, showing the values of `a`, `b`, `i` and any output.

```
a ← 2
b ← 1
FOR i ← 1 TO 3
   b ← b * a
   a ← a + 1
ENDFOR
OUTPUT b
```
questions.solution: Write the value of a variable only when it changes, one row per pass through the loop, with the output in its own column.

criteria.text: Row for i = 3: b = 24, a = 5, then output 24

questions.modelAnswer:
| i | a | b | output |
|---|---|---|---|
|   | 2 | 1 |   |
| 1 | 3 | 2 |   |
| 2 | 4 | 6 |   |
| 3 | 5 | 24 |   |
|   |   |   | 24 |

Each pass multiplies `b` by the current `a` **before** `a` goes up: $1 \times 2 = 2$, then $2 \times 3 = 6$, then $6 \times 4 = 24$. The order of the two lines inside the loop is the point of the question; swapping them would give $3 \times 4 \times 5 = 60$.

questions.prompt:
What is output by this program?

```
SUBROUTINE g(n)
   RETURN n + 3
ENDSUBROUTINE

SUBROUTINE f(n)
   RETURN n * n
ENDSUBROUTINE

OUTPUT f(g(2))
```
questions.solution: Work from the inside out. `g(2)` returns 2 + 3 = 5. Then `f(5)` returns 5 × 5 = 25.

questions.prompt: Two students write a program that converts prices from pounds to euros in six different places. Student A writes the calculation out each time. Student B writes one function `to_euros(pounds)` and calls it six times. The exchange rate changes. Which statement is correct?
questions.solution: One definition, one change. That is the reuse argument for subroutines in a concrete case.
options: Student B changes one line inside the function; Student A must find and change all six calculations and may miss one
Student B's program cannot be changed without rewriting all six calls
Both programs need six changes, because the function is called six times and each call has to be edited to pass the new exchange rate
Student A's program is easier to update because every calculation is visible at the place it is used, so each one can be checked as it is changed

questions.prompt: Which of these is part of the structured approach to programming?
questions.solution: The structured approach splits a program into subroutines, each with a clear, documented interface: **parameters in, a return value out, local variables inside**. Globals everywhere, one long program and copied code are what it replaces.
options: Subroutines with clear interfaces: parameters in, a return value out, local variables inside
Global variables for every value, so that any subroutine can read and change what it needs
One long main program, so the whole solution can be read from top to bottom at once
Copying a block of code into each place it is needed, so every copy can be tuned

questions.prompt:
What is output by this program?

```
SUBROUTINE calc(a, b)
   RETURN a - b * 2
ENDSUBROUTINE

x ← 10
y ← 3
OUTPUT calc(y, x)
```
questions.solution: Values are matched to the parameters in order, not by name: `calc(y, x)` makes a = 3 and b = 10. Multiplication comes before subtraction, so the function returns 3 − 10 × 2 = 3 − 20 = **−17**.

markScheme.description: a = 3 and b = 10, matched in order

questions.prompt:
What is output by this program?

```
SUBROUTINE grade(mark)
   IF mark ≥ 50 THEN
      RETURN 'Pass'
   ELSE
      RETURN 'Fail'
   ENDIF
ENDSUBROUTINE

OUTPUT grade(49) + grade(50)
```
questions.solution: 49 is less than 50, so `grade(49)` returns 'Fail'. 50 ≥ 50 is true, so `grade(50)` returns 'Pass'. The two strings are joined with nothing between them: **FailPass**.

markScheme.description: grade(49) returns Fail and grade(50) returns Pass

questions.prompt: Which of these subroutines is a function?
questions.solution: In AQA pseudo-code a subroutine that contains `RETURN` is a function. Only `twice`, whose body is `RETURN x * 2`, hands a value back; the others output or store a value and return nothing, so they are procedures.
options: `SUBROUTINE show(x)` whose whole body is `OUTPUT x * 2`
`SUBROUTINE twice(x)` whose body is `RETURN x * 2`
`SUBROUTINE hello()` whose body is `OUTPUT 'Hi'`
`SUBROUTINE store(x)` whose body is `y ← x * 2`

examTechnique.body: Paper 1 tests subroutines three ways: trace a call and state what is returned or output, explain why subroutines are used, and write a subroutine to a specification. For tracing, draw the table with a column per variable and fill it row by row. For writing, get the header, the parameters and the RETURN right first; those are the core of the answer. Coded answers are written in the language your paper is set in (Python, C# or VB.NET); algorithm questions can be answered in clear pseudo-code.
examinerErrors: Outputting inside a function instead of returning the value.
Forgetting RETURN in one branch of an IF, so the function sometimes returns nothing.
Worrying about parameters against arguments. AQA states it uses **parameter** for both, so do not lose time drawing a distinction the board does not examine.
Treating a variable assigned inside a subroutine as if it changed the global one.
Writing the answer to a trace question without the trace table. The table shows your working, so a slip can be found and put right.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer traces nested calls from the inside out with every value in the table, writes functions that return in every branch and never output, explains the reuse and testing benefits with a concrete example, and keeps local and global variables apart.
